terms.definition: A configured chain of receivers, processors and exporters that telemetry flows through. Pipelines are declared under `service.pipelines` in the collector configuration, one per signal, and components are wired into them by their type id.
A component that ingests telemetry from a source — a socket, a file, an API or a scrape target — and passes it into the pipeline. Its `status.class` in metadata.yaml is `receiver`.
A component that sits between receivers and exporters to transform, filter, sample, batch or enrich telemetry before it leaves the collector.
A component that terminates a pipeline by sending telemetry to a backend such as an OTLP endpoint, a Prometheus-compatible store or a message queue.

A component that provides capabilities outside the telemetry pipeline itself — authentication, health checks, storage, service observers and OpAMP — and therefore attaches to the service rather than to a pipeline.
A component that consumes from one pipeline and produces into another, either bridging signals (for example traces to metrics) or fanning a single stream out to several destinations.

A component that pulls metrics from a target on an interval. Scrapers are not pipelines themselves: they are composed into receivers such as the hostmetrics receiver, and `scraper` is its own component class in contrib.

The interface a component implements to receive telemetry from the stage before it in a pipeline. Connectors are consumers of one pipeline and producers of another, which is what lets them bridge signals.

The kind of telemetry being carried: traces, metrics or logs (profiles are a fourth, still-emerging signal). Each component declares per-signal support, so it can be stable for one signal and alpha for another.

The OpenTelemetry Protocol — the wire format and transport used to exchange signals between collectors and between collectors and backends. Several contrib components encode, decode or relay OTLP payloads.

The maturity level of a component for a given signal, declared under `status.stability` in metadata.yaml. It sets user expectations and gates which distributions may ship the component; maintainers may downgrade components deemed unmaintained or risky.
A shipped collector build. distributions.yaml lists the ones a component may belong to — core, contrib, k8s and otlp — and metadata.yaml records which of them actually include the component.

Whether a component is compiled into a given distribution. Membership is declared in metadata.yaml, reflected in README status tables, and made real by listing the component in the distribution's builder config such as cmd/otelcontribcol/builder-config.yaml.
The configuration-mapping layer that loads collector YAML and resolves config URIs into typed Go configuration. Providers under confmap/ teach it new URI schemes, for example `s3://` bucket objects.

The source file that registers a component with the collector: it creates default configuration, exposes the component's type id and constructs the runtime instance. Every component follows the same config and factory layout.

The metadata generator driven by a component's metadata.yaml: `make generate` / `make mdatagen` produces the README status section, documentation.md and the generated tests (for example generated_component_test.go). Repo-wide behaviour — test exclusions and stability coverage thresholds — is configured in .mdatagen.yaml.

The machine-readable manifest at the root of every component directory: type, display name, description, status (class, stability, distributions, codeowners) and feature gates. It is the source of truth the atlas extracts components from.
A runtime toggle that keeps unfinished or risky behaviour off the default code path until it is ready. Components declare their gates in metadata.yaml and users flip them with `--feature-gates`.
What a component declares it can handle — in contrib processors most often `consumer.Capabilities{MutatesData: true}`, which tells the collector the component may modify the telemetry it receives.

The generated .github/CODEOWNERS file mapping every component path to the people who maintain it. GitHub requests them as reviewers automatically, and metadata.yaml is where the active and emeritus lists are edited.

The directory holding one YAML changelog entry per user-facing change. `make chlog-new` copies the template, `make chlog-validate` checks it, and at release time chloggen folds every entry into CHANGELOG.md or CHANGELOG-API.md and deletes it.

The `status` block of metadata.yaml describes what a component *is* — its class, distributions and code owners (including the `seeking_new` flag) — while stability describes how mature it is *per signal*: a receiver can declare beta stability for metrics while the logs it emits stay in development.

The controlled environment under testbed/ for end-to-end, correctness, stability and load tests of the collector: a load generator feeds data to the component under test while a mock backend receives and asserts on it.
The goroutine-leak checker wired into generated component tests. mdatagen adds it per component and .mdatagen.yaml records the components that are exempt from it.
The machine-checkable description of a component's configuration, generated as config.schema.yaml next to the Go config struct so tooling can validate and document user configuration.

The generator that turns a component's Go configuration structs into its config.schema.yaml. The tool itself lives in the core collector (`go.opentelemetry.io/collector/cmd/schemagen`, invoked through `make schemagen`); .schemagen.yaml supplies the type mappings, allowed external refs and per-component overrides that steer it.

Every component directory carries its own go.mod, so a custom build of the collector can pull in only the dependencies it needs. `make crosslink` keeps intra-repo `replace` directives in sync so the module resolves during development.
The tool that inserts `replace` statements into the go.mod of every intra-repository dependent, which is what makes a new component resolvable when the contrib executable is built.

Go build constraints that keep long-running tests out of the default test run. `integration` tests can run locally without credentials and are executed by CI; `e2e` tests are wired per component in .github/workflows.

A contributor with triager permissions who helps issues along: adding the missing component labels that organise issues and trigger the automations notifying code owners, investigating reports directly, or pointing issue authors at someone who can.

The vocabulary issues are classified with — bug, enhancement, good first issue, help wanted, needs triage, waiting-for-codeowners and priority levels — documented in issue-triaging.md and applied by triagers or by automation.

A comment starting with `/label` followed by space-separated label names that applies those labels to an issue or pull request, letting code owners manage labels without triager permissions. Prefix with `-` to remove one.

The label marking work that needs no specialised or in-depth knowledge of a component and is therefore ideal for a first-time contributor. Its neighbour `help wanted` marks issues whose code owners do not expect to have time for them soon.
The section structure every pull request inherits: description, link to tracking issue, testing, documentation and an authorship attestation that the human author must tick themselves.

Pull request titles start with the component type and name in brackets followed by a short statement — for example `[processor/tailsampling] fix AND policy` — or read `as per changelog` when a changelog entry already describes the change.

The maintainer or approver automatically assigned to help a pull request reach merge: keeping review moving, supplying the official approval when reviewers lack approval rights, and merging it as a maintainer. The `ready to merge` label is set only once an approver has approved.
The set of modules a pull request's CI actually runs. A script inspects the diff and emits either named test groups or bucketed module paths; the `ci:full` label forces the full matrix.

The process of moving a component built outside this repository into contrib: open an issue with a sponsor and at least three code owners, agree the plan, then land it as a series of pull requests ending with alpha stability.

Make targets are split so that module-level targets (in Makefile.Common) act on one Go module, while repo-level targets in the root Makefile wrap them across every module — `make lint` is scoped, `make golint` covers the whole repository.
